audacious

aw-DAY-shus -- from Latin audere, 'to dare': an audacious act is one that took real daring to attempt. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Audacious is strikingly bold, in a way that can seem admirable or reckless.

It was an audacious bet for the small startup to challenge the industry's biggest company to a public product contest.

Example

With no climbing experience and no permit, the teenager made the audacious climb up the abandoned water tower in full view of the town, just to prove it could be done.

Audacious captures boldness so extreme that it can seem admirable, reckless, or both at once -- climbing an unpermitted tower in full public view is exactly the kind of daring, attention-grabbing act the word describes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

daring: Daring puts the accent on the risk itself and most naturally describes physical feats -- dives, rescues, stunts. Audacious ranges wider, fitting bold plans, words, and ideas just as easily, and it adds a jolt of shock at the sheer nerve involved.

adventurous: Adventurous describes a taste for new experiences -- new trails, new foods, unfamiliar cities -- and the risks involved can be quite small. Audacious is bigger and louder: boldness striking enough to shock onlookers, whether they end up applauding it or calling it reckless.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

timid: showing a lack of courage or confidence

cautious: careful to avoid danger or risk

Where it sits · how shocking the risk-taking is — bold → audacious → foolhardy

bold vs. audacious: Bold is a common, everyday word for confident risk-taking, while audacious pushes further, suggesting boldness so extreme it might shock people.

foolhardy vs. audacious: Foolhardy pushes past audacious into outright folly -- boldness so heedless of danger that it stops looking impressive and starts looking senseless.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — audac-

root — audac-: bold, to dare (Latin audere)

suffix — -ious

suffix — -ious: full of, characterized by (Latin -osus)

Put it together

Put it together: Audacious comes from Latin audere, 'to dare' -- worth noting that this is a different root from audio and audible, which come from audire, 'to hear'; despite the similar spelling, audacious has nothing to do with sound. The noun form audacity shares the exact same 'to dare' root.

Use the root in a new word: audacity

Use the root in a new word: audacity: Nobody could believe the audacity of the plan, but somehow it actually worked.

Word Choice

Audacious describes striking boldness whose tone can be admiring or critical depending on context, unlike "brash," which is always at least a little bit critical, adding rudeness or a lack of tact to the boldness.
